name: image/vnd.microsoft.icon
description:
The Windows icon format. An ICO file is a container. It holds several complete images at different sizes and colour depths, and the consumer picks whichever fits the space it needs to fill. That is how one `favicon.ico` serves both a 16-pixel browser tab and a 48-pixel desktop shortcut.

Images inside are stored either as BMP data or, since Windows Vista, as [image/png](/image/png).

The labelling is inconsistent. `image/vnd.microsoft.icon` is the registered type, but browsers and web servers overwhelmingly send [image/x-icon](/image/x-icon) instead. Both are accepted.

name: image/emf
description:
EMF, the Enhanced Metafile format, records a drawing as a replayable list of Windows GDI calls rather than as pixels. GDI is the Graphics Device Interface, the drawing layer of Windows, and the calls are lines, curves, text and fills that scale cleanly to any resolution.

It is registered by RFC 7903 and documented publicly as `[MS-EMF]`, one of Microsoft's open specifications. It is the format placed on the clipboard when vector artwork is copied between Windows applications, and the one Office embeds when a chart or diagram is pasted into a document.

RFC 7903 also records `image/x-emf` as deprecated in favour of this type.

name: image/wmf
description:
WMF is the original Windows Metafile format, the 16-bit predecessor to [image/emf](/image/emf), introduced with Windows 3.x. Like the Enhanced Metafile format it stores a sequence of Graphics Device Interface drawing commands rather than a bitmap, so the output scales. Its older record set is much more limited.

It is registered by RFC 7903 and documented as `[MS-WMF]`, one of Microsoft's open specifications. You still find it inside older Office documents and clip-art libraries.

RFC 7903 also records `image/x-wmf` as deprecated in favour of this type.

name: image/dpx
description:
DPX (Digital Picture Exchange) stores a single motion picture frame. It is standardised as ST 268-1 by the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers. A sequence is a directory of numbered files, one per frame, which is how film scanners and digital intermediate pipelines pass work between tools.

The header carries the metadata a post-production facility needs: timecode, film edge codes and the transfer characteristic. The pixel data is typically 10 bits per channel, in a logarithmic encoding that preserves highlight detail the way a film negative does.

It began as an evolution of Kodak's Cineon format and is still the standard way to exchange uncompressed frames.

name: image/aces
description:
The ACES image container file layout, standardised as ST 2065-4 by the Society of Motion Picture and Television Engineers. ACES is the Academy Color Encoding System. The container is a constrained profile of OpenEXR: the same file structure, with colour space, channel naming and required attributes pinned down so any ACES-compliant tool reads the contents identically.

That constraint is the reason it exists. ACES makes colour behave predictably as footage moves between facilities, and a container permitting fewer choices is easier to be strict about.

Watch the extension. Files use `.exr`, the same as ordinary OpenEXR images, so the extension alone will not tell you whether a file follows the ACES profile.

name: image/vnd.radiance
description:
Radiance HDR stores high dynamic range images. It is commonly called RGBE after its encoding: each pixel gets three 8-bit mantissas for red, green and blue, plus one shared 8-bit exponent. Four bytes per pixel covers a range of many orders of magnitude, enough to hold both deep shadow and direct sun in one image.

It came out of the Radiance lighting simulation package at Lawrence Berkeley Laboratory. It became the common format for environment maps and image-based lighting in 3D rendering.

IANA registers no extension for it. `.hdr` is the most common, with `.pic`, `.rgbe` and `.xyze` also in use. `.pic` is ambiguous and worth avoiding.

name: image/fits
description:
FITS, the Flexible Image Transport System, is the standard data format of astronomy. RFC 4047 registers it, and the International Astronomical Union maintains it. A file is a sequence of header-and-data units: a human-readable ASCII header of keyword and value pairs, followed by an n-dimensional array.

It is not only an image format. The array may be a photograph from a telescope, but it may equally be a spectrum, a data cube or a table. The header carries the calibration and coordinate information needed to interpret it scientifically.

Backwards compatibility is a stated design principle. Files written decades ago still read correctly, which matters when the observations cannot be repeated.

furtherReading.title: RFC 4047 - MIME Sub-type Registrations for FITS

name: image/tiff-fx
description:
TIFF-FX is the image format for internet fax. RFC 3950 registers it, and RFC 3949 defines the file format itself. It is a constrained profile of [image/tiff](/image/tiff): a specific set of compression schemes, resolutions and tags that a receiving fax device is guaranteed to understand.

The profiles run from plain black and white at fax resolution up to colour coded with JPEG or with JBIG, the Joint Bi-level Image Experts Group scheme. Restricting the parent format this way is what makes interoperability possible between devices that share nothing else.

It is the payload carried by the email-based fax profiles rather than a format anyone authors directly.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3950 - Tag Image File Format Fax eXtended (TIFF-FX)

name: image/t38
description:
T.38 is the ITU-T recommendation for carrying fax over IP networks in real time. This media type, registered by RFC 3362, labels the image data within it.

A T.38 gateway does not digitise the fax tones as audio and hope they survive transcoding. It demodulates the fax at one end, sends the page data over IP, and remodulates it at the other. That is what makes faxing work over voice over IP at all.

You will find this type inside session descriptions for SIP, the Session Initiation Protocol, rather than as a file on disk.

furtherReading.title: RFC 3362 - Real-time Facsimile (T.38) - image/t38 MIME Sub-type Registration

name: image/vnd.zbrush.pcx
description:
A Pixologic registration for the PCX files written by ZBrush, the digital sculpting application. PCX itself is a much older ZSoft format from the 1980s, covered on this site at [image/x-pcx](/image/x-pcx).

The registration exists to give ZBrush's variant its own label. Public documentation of how it differs from ordinary PCX is thin, so treat the distinction as a vendor claim rather than a described format difference.

The practical consequence is the extension clash: a `.pcx` file may be either, and the extension alone will not tell you which.
